title: Migrant Workers in Surat Fight for Rest and Fair Wages
description: Surat’s embroidery workers face dismissals and police action for demanding weekly offs and overtime pay. Explore the class struggle behind their fight for labour rights.
author: Gautam  Nirmal Doshi
content:
In one of the many power looms of Surat’s sprawling textile industry, Vishal Baghi, a 25-year-old from Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, has spent over four years working 12-hour-shifts in the embroidery line. In late August, at around 11 pm, Baghi was fired by his employer. This was the second time he was fired in less than two weeks. The reason: demanding a weekly day off from work.
“I was removed [from my job] only because I was raising awareness for a weekly off and for reasonable shifts,” Baghi said. He showed his social media profile with videos of him speaking at gatherings of migrant workers who are made to work 12-hour shifts each day, throughout the year, with three days off in a year at most.
The migrant embroidery workers started agitating on August 16, with weekly off as the primary demand. As per a report by The Indian Express, the protest began at the embroidery units of the Vedanta industrial area in Amroli, Surat. Soon, it spread to Anjani Industries, Katargam, Sachin GIDC, Pipodara, and Kadodara. Workers halted operations and staged demonstrations in other factories as well. An FIR was registered against 500 workers at the Amroli police station on August 17. Violence was also reported in some areas, and eight persons were arrested, as per the report.
Talks between the factory owners and the authorities followed. The workers’ demands were met with a lacklustre response from the owners. Now, the situation has worsened for the workers with the police detaining some of them and a few even losing their jobs because of their participation in gatherings and demonstrations.
“I was fired on that day [August 16] itself for participating in the dharna. Not one owner spoke to us. Instead, they recorded the protests with on phones. Over the next few days, at least 200 workers were fired because they were seen in these protests and demonstrations,” Baghi told Frontline.
Also Read | A new blow to workers
As per news reports, a memorandum submitted to the police by Janmabhumi Bharat Majdoor Union president Ajay Dubey states that the approximately 18 lakh migrant workers in Surat’s textile industry do not get benefits such as provident fund, insurance, and gratuity.
Surat is one of India’s most concentrated textile hubs and employs over 20 lakh workers. According to the Surat International Textile Expo (SITEX), an initiative of the Southern Gujarat Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SGCCI), approximately 65 per cent of the country’s synthetic textiles are produced in Surat with an annual sales value of Rs.85,000 crore. Production, in value terms, has been growing at the rate of 12 per cent per annum.
The advent and installation of automatic machines have been pivotal to the transformation of the sector in Surat. Labour-intensive tasks such as weaving and embroidery are now mechanised, requiring fewer but better skilled workers. There are 1.5 lakh embroidery machines, as per SITEX, spread across the city, with factories working round-the-clock, with workers across two 12-hour shifts.
Demands of workers
On October 23, the workers gathered at Citi Industrial Estate in Udhna, Surat, to negotiate with one of the factory owners about the continuation of their employment and weekly offs. The demands of the workers Frontline met were fairly simple. First, one weekly day off from the rigorous routine. Second, 8-hour shifts with compensation for overtime work, with an additional half-a-day wage for a 12-hour shift. Third, timely payment in the first week of the month, as opposed to irregular payment in the third or fourth week as is the case sometimes, according to a few workers.
Kamalnath Kushwaha, an embroidery worker from Satna in Madhya Pradesh who has been in Surat for at least 12 years, said, “We are not asking for a common day off [like Sunday] for everyone. You can give people different off-days so that work doesn’t stop. This is a simple demand.”
Rohit, a factory worker in Udhna, said, “We were not given a holiday on August 15 [Independence Day] either. When everyone else celebrates by hoisting and waving our country’s flag, don’t we have the right to get the day off and celebrate as well? But, instead, we worked 12-hour shifts as usual. Are we not humans?”
Kushwaha added, “We were not even given two hours off to go out. It’s ironic because it was Independence Day.”
Rohit has been working in Surat for over 15 years, and now has a wife and a young daughter. “I don’t get time to spend with my little daughter at all. We finish work at 8:30 pm, head home, do our daily chores, and then we’re just exhausted. It’s difficult to wake up again and head straight to work when you’re so tired. We’re just asking for a day off so that we can rest and recuperate,” he said, asking for the weekly off even if no other is demand is met.
Baghi, who is unmarried, said it is hard to do anything besides work: “I go home, make dinner, and it’s late by the time I eat and clean. I wake up at 7 am, prepare and pack my lunch and rush to work. I don’t get time to speak to my family back home [in Mirzapur] who go to sleep before I finish my chores.”
For the workers, leisure is a dream. Baghi and the others said they rarely even go to a park or meet friends, which would require sacrificing their much-needed sleep. “I know very few places in Surat because I haven’t explored it at all, despite being here for over 4 years,” said Baghi. Embroidery workers in Surat earn between Rs.20,000 to Rs.30,000, depending on their experience and the type of work and machine they handle.
A choice that wasn’t
Following weeks of unsuccessful attempts since August to get their demands met, the workers along with labour union leaders like Malkhan Singh Verma, president of the Sarvajanik Mazdoor Ekta Union, had notified the authorities that they would stage a peaceful protest on October 1. On September 29, the office of the Deputy Labour Commissioner in Surat sent a letter to the Textile Embroidery Jobwork Association of Surat (TEJAS), a non-profit trade association for embroidery factory owners and entrepreneurs, and to the SGCCI. It directed the organisations to implement the provisions of the four labour codes: The Code of Wages, 2019; The Occupational Safety, Health, and Working Conditions Code, 2020; The Code on Social Security, 2020; and The Industrial Relations Code, 2020.
The letter stated that “provisions have been made for wages, working hours and holidays as per the Wages Code, 2019 and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Therefore, all the members associated with your association are requested to take action as per the provisions of the labour codes and to inform you accordingly so that the labour codes can be implemented smoothly. If any legal guidance is required in this regard, you are advised to contact this office”.
Verma said, “The workers were happy with this letter, and the protest stopped too. But the owners were still not meeting the demands. They are running these factories as per their own rules and regulations, and don’t want to change that. The migrant workers from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, and other States work according to what other workers, who are not aware of the [labour] laws, tell them.”
On October 10 and 11, TEJAS offered a resolution for the concerns around wages, shift structure, and other operational guidelines. As per local news reports, its unanimous decision was that if embroidery karigars (skilled workers) wished to work as per rules, they will be paid Rs.550 for an 8-hour shift, instead of the minimum wage of Rs.522. Alternatively, they can opt for the existing system of a monthly salary between Rs.25,000 and Rs.30,000, based on performance.
Additionally, TEJAS placed a ban on mobile phones on factory floors. It said that if the factory owner suffers any loss due to the use of mobile phones, 50 per cent of the loss amount must be paid by the worker concerned. Now, effectively, if a worker opts for the 8-hour shift system (48 hours per week), the monthly wage will be Rs.14,300, factoring in the four weekly offs without compensation.
As per the Union Ministry of Labour and Employment’s Code on Wages, 2019, and The Occupational Safety, Health, and Working Conditions Code, 2020, workers are eligible for
• a “day of rest in every period of seven days which shall be allowed to all employees or to any specified class of employees and for the payment of remuneration in respect of such days of rest”; and
• wages at the rate of twice the rate of wages for overtime work.
Additionally, as per The Gujarat Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) (Amendment) Act, 2026, which amended the 2019 Act, no worker shall be required or allowed to work for more than 10 hours a day and 48 hours a week. But embroidery workers in Surat work 12 hours a day and 84 hours a week.
The resolution offered by TEJAS allows workers to opt for 48-hour work weeks, with a day off, but at a salary of just Rs.14,300, with no remuneration for rest days as per Union Ministry of Labour and Employment’s stipulated guidelines. However, some workers do think that if they are paid overtime, this could still work.
Rohit said, “We are okay with the decision [of Rs.550 per day] if we get paid overtime for 12 hour shifts. They will need three sets of workers for 8-hour shifts so that the factories can run round-the-clock. Getting so many additional workers is difficult. So they will have to continue with two sets of workers, and if we get paid for overtime, then we are okay with this.”
Four hours of overtime at twice the wage rate would add up to Rs.1,100 every day, or Rs.28,600 for a 30-day period with four days off and 24 hours of overtime per week. But this rests on the hope of getting the stipulated overtime wage rate, which TEJAS has said nothing about. Verma said: “The workers are asking at the least, a weekly off, as per the labour laws. They are not asking for a stake in the ownership of the factory. Why does TEJAS need to intervene?”
He added, “The workers don’t get an ID card, payslip, gratuity, bonuses, or anything. So, if you want to give them Rs.550 for an 8-hour shift as per the stipulated rules, what about the rest [of the rules]?”
Surveillance, loss of work, and lack of dignity
The workers alleged that those who participated in protests and gatherings have been surveilled through recordings on smartphones, and their photos, videos, and details like names are being shared with groups of factory owners.
Kushwaha said, “I was removed from my job on October 4 on the pretext that I was asking for weekly offs. In a few days, I got a job elsewhere and just as it was being finalised, I got a call that they could not hire me. The only logical explanation is that the owners communicate among themselves, and we are blacklisted because of our simple demands.”
Baghi also uploads videos of his speeches and interviews with other workers on social media. A few days after being fired on August 16, he got a job at another factory. But he was fired again, on the first day of work.
He said, “The owners have recordings of the protests, and our details, and share our videos and profiles on their [chat] groups. We are not selected [for work] anywhere. There are some who went back to their villages after being fired, but many have stayed, hoping they will get work somewhere and send money back home.”
Speaking about the humiliation of workers, Verma said, “No one can be expected to work 365 days a year. Please think of these skilled workers as humans.”
Senior national spokesperson of the Indian Youth Congress and labour activist Shaan Khan stated that the work requires a lot of effort, despite the technological developments.
Frontline visited a factory floor in an embroidery unit in Surat at around 10 pm, when a worker was operating a large machine with over 20 units, each comprising different heads for different beads and decorative accessories.
The temperature on factory floors in the area is regulated through windowless openings in walls, but the heat and noise near the machines are still significantly high. The worker has to know his way around the machine’s software to start the process. It must also be halted for several reasons, such as inserting more thread, beads, and so on.
Baghi said, “The machines always stay on. Even during lunch, we are not allowed to go together. If I leave, the worker on the adjacent machine looks after mine as well. And I do the same for him.”
In one embroidery unit, a small place to cook is located right outside the bathroom. A worker who did not wish to be named said, “The working conditions are really bad.” He was neither wearing gloves nor any safety gear.
Verma said, “There is no provision for workers’ safety in these units. Gloves, helmet, eye-protection wear, nothing is given.” Across the power loom with this embroidery unit, workers were easing into their night shifts that day.
Lathicharge and preventive detentions
With their demands not met and the half-hearted response of TEJAS, on October 15, the workers, union leaders, and activists staged a peaceful protest march towards the Collector’s office. They had requested permission from the police but were not given one. The protest was not called off, and this led to preventive detentions of Khan, Baghi, and Verma.
Khan said, “I was picked up on the night of October 14 itself.” Baghi was detained at around 11 pm the same night. “I was let go the next evening and was not able to participate in the protest. From the night of October 14 until 10 am the next day, people were detained successively.”
Verma said, “I was called to the police station at 7 am for a chat but wasn’t allowed to leave until 8 pm.” He added, “Those not detained who participated in the protest were met with hundreds of police personnel outside the Collector’s office, as if they were some sort of criminals.” Verma, Baghi, and Khan said that there was a lathicharge, and some workers were hurt. The workers believe that the authorities are complicit with the factory owners because of how the events unfolded.
Govind, who hails from Deoria in Uttar Pradesh and has been in Surat for several years, was also detained during the protest. He said, “Almost 90 of us were detained and not released until that evening. With their [TEJAS’] response, it is clear that even the authorities might be okay with this because they are not making efforts to implement the provisions in the [labour] laws.”
Govind said he was fired on October 15 due to his participation in the protest. “I spoke to them and I’m starting again tomorrow [October 24]. But several workers were fired, and many are planning to go back home. We are labelled as outsiders but we’ve spent our entire childhood in Surat, working. Now, even our kids study in schools here,” he said. TEJAS facilitated a gathering of around 25,000 embroidery workers on October 10. The workers were disappointed that they could not do the same without a confrontation with the police.
Deflated hope and the way forward
Union Minister of Textiles Giriraj Singh visited Surat on October 9 and 10, and as per news reports, his only comment was that the workers and owners should resolve the issues through dialogue. On October 14, as per news reports, union leader Dubey was arrested on charges of extorting a trader. He was released last week, but this has dented his credibility among workers. Nevertheless, most workers remain undeterred in their struggle for better working conditions.
TEJAS’s Karunesh Ranpariya has posted videos about the workers’ and factory owners’ disagreements on his social media profile. In one post, he wrote that “workers go to the machine owner’s place to operate the machine on their own will. The worker sees the machine, the design running—suit, sari, chaniya [lehenga], or garment—and the worker and owner mutually agree on a salary for 30 days. This has been the system for more than 30 years.” He blamed the union leaders “who neither operate the machine nor are machine owners, [but] create conflicts between workers and owners by raising the issue of an 8-hour shift and holidays on Sunday just to run their own shop.”
Also Read | Dictatorship of the employer?
He also posted videos of CCTV footage from a factory floor of a worker manhandling an embroidery machine. He further said that owners have identified other non-workers “causing outrage” about the issue, and even noted that TEJAS would support embroidery machine owners and make them its members if they sign up with a cancelled cheque.
According to Gujarati news reports, Ranpariya was one of five people accused of embezzling crores in donations under the name of “various social organisations in Surat”, including TEJAS. He was arrested in Madhya Pradesh in June 2023 after the investigation was handed over to the Amroli police station. As per his social media posts, he joined the BJP in November 2023.
Baghi said, “If I go home, I’ll have to work in construction with a pay of Rs.400 at most, that too in a place 25 km away. I have to find work here because I’m not experienced in anything else.”
While the workers have other demands, the primary one is just a weekly day off. At Citi Industrial Estate on October 23, one of the workers said, “The owner agreed to give us two paid days off in a month. We should have taken that.” Seemingly, a weekly day off would be far-fetched.

title: TVK’s Muslim appeasement on full display: Tamil Nadu govt apologises, blames Devasthanam’s non-approval for breach of SC order; petitioners point to “deliberate attempt at non-compliance”
description: The TVK govt of Tamil Nadu furnished a status report on the issue and blamed the tustees for disregarding the SC order. | OpIndia News
category: Editor's picks, Featured, News Reports, Opinions, Politics
author: Rukma Rathore
content:
On 25th November (Wednesday), the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government of Tamil Nadu apologised in the Supreme Court after it lit the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the traditional Uchipillayar Deepa Mandapam rather than the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram hill, in violation of its order.
Notably, the government was instructed to use the stone pillar for the ceremonial lamp ceremony by both the Supreme Court and the Madras High Court. Now, the apex court has stated that it will review the state government’s status report on the issue alongside considering the contempt plea presented by the petitioners.
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan initially brought up the matter on behalf of the authorities, before a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi, conveying, “As the Collector, I was supposed to file a status report on what took place. We have just had that filed. We have a number. I think Your Lordships may take it up because unfortunately the lamp didn’t get lit. So I, as a Collector, have traced out all the steps that I was supposed to comply with.”
The state claimed that the order was not executed because of the Board of Trustees. It alleged, “I sincerely apologise for the lamp not being lit at the Deepathoon. The district administration made every effort to secure the authorisation of the Devasthanam and the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon. However, the Board of Trustees, by its resolution dated 24th November, resolved to light the lamp at the customary place. I will submit an additional status report with all supporting documents along with the same.”
The state argued that “every arrangement was complete and every possible difficulty had been offered an immediate solution” by the district administration, adding, “The only step remaining was the authorisation of the team by the Devasthanam. The time for the ceremony was fixed at 6.00 pm to 6:30 pm as proposed by the Executive Officer herself. No team authorised by the Devasthanam came forward within that time, and no request for any extension of time was received. At 7:32 pm, the temple’s press release was received.”
Afterwards, the Executive Officer asserted that she could not intervene because of a resolution passed by the trustees.
#BREAKING Madurai District Collector tells #SupremeCourt that all arrangements were made by the District Administration to light the Kartigai Deepam at the Thiruparankundram Deepathoon. However, it could not be lit there as the Board of Trustees of the Temple Devasthanam did not authorise the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon, as they took the stance that it can be lit only where it was being customarily done at the Uchaipillaiyar Mandapam.
— Live Law (@LiveLawIndia) November 25, 2026
Petitioners expose the government’s dubious conduct
Senior lawyer Guru Krishna Kumar, who represented the Hindu petitioners, called out the deceptive tactics of the government and charged, “This is like anticipatory breach, anticipatory mentioning. Most unfortunate, My Lords. State tells the High Court some prohibitory orders were. They use the Board of Trustees, and I say this, to say the custom does not permit it, and the sthanikars have said it cannot be done.”
He further stated that the government and the devasthanam joined hands to defend the contravention of the verdict and mentioned, “In the evening, later, sthanikars say that ‘no, we didn’t make any such statement; no opinion was sought from us.’ Deliberate attempt at not complying with the order, and they’ve succeeded by stratagem and devices. Most unfortunate. There is a complete infraction of the rule of law. This is the majesty of the law that we are looking at.”
The petitioners demanded to start suo motu contempt proceedings, and direct that the flame currently burning at the conventional location be moved to the Deepathoon. They also highlighted how the state government consistently promised the High Court that it would implement the ruling, right up until the last moment, only to willfully fail to carry it out under the guise of trustees. “You file the necessary plea. You take the steps. We will consider,” responded Justice Aravind Kumar.
No lengths too far for Muslim appeasement
The TVK government had already expressed its objection to the court’s resolution through its review petition. The measure to brazenly disregard it predictably did not originate from any independent decision by the Devasthanam or its trustees, who function under the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Department, which has long faced allegations of exploiting temple funds, undermining Hindu traditions and interfering in religious affairs.
The institution being made a scapegoat in this case is not an independent body but one that operates under the state government’s control. As the petitioners had already pointed out, this was nothing more than a collusive effort by the two sides to create a smoke-and-mirrors show.
The glaring truth that the government is attempting to obscure through its absurd explanations is that the TVK, much like its predecessor, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which wanted to eradicate Sanatan Dharma, is following the well-worn formula of “secularism” centred on pandering to Muslims.
The latter invoked the purported need to “preserve law and order” and “prevent communal tensions” to justify flouting the High Court judgement and preventing Hindu devotees from lighting the lamp at the stone pillar last year. The more things have changed, the more they visibly stayed the same.
The TVK government is pursuing the route set by its predecessor, willing to compromise not only Hindu religious rights and faith but also showing little regard for even the courts of the country. Moreover, alliance partners including the Indian National Congress, Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK), Communist Party of India (Marxist), Communist Party of India (CPI) and Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) put tremendous pressure to disobey the judicial mandate.
The action has already faced fierce opposition from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Hindu groups for its vote bank motive. A similar instance of this was observed earlier this month, when the Joseph Vijay-led government in Tamil Nadu decided to regularise encroachments by issuing pattas to thousands of mosques, churches and dargahs.
According to A M Shah Jahan, Minister for Minorities Welfare, the government was working to regularise religious institutions that lack ownership documentation. He informed that minority groups petitioned the government for pattas for unlawful houses of worship that had been on government property for 25-50 years.
Hence, a decision was made to comply with the demands of Christians and Muslims, and the required paperwork would be completed shortly. To cater to its vote bank, the government has even given the green light to illegal occupation, setting a deeply troubling and equally dangerous precedent.
Furthermore, the government has been accused of diverting public funds towards freebies and schemes targeting its Muslim vote bank even as the state’s coffers come under strain. It has set aside Rs 20 crore for female students from the community and announced the expansion of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board scholarship for Muslim girls from Classes 1-8 to Classes 9-10 at Rs 2,000 per year, totalling Rs 8.28 crore.
Tamil Nadu also introduced a Rs 100 crore interest-free revolving amount to provide loans for developing income-generating assets on Muslim and Christian properties, and allocated an estimated Rs 40 crore for a new headquarters for the state Waqf Board while raising its administrative grant to Rs 5 crore.
On the other hand, the Joseph Vijay-led coalition did not even allow the lighting of a lamp on the stone pillar on a single occasion, as pronounced by the Supreme Court.
In this political calculus, Hindus, along with their rights and religious beliefs, are turned into soft targets by these self-proclaimed secularists, while the authority of the courts is rendered virtually meaningless. It would not be wrong to call this yet another low point, shameful but hardly surprising, in India’s brand of “secular politics,” where even the judiciary is sacrificed at the altar of Muslim appeasement.
The comrades in the media have commenced the whitewashing, carefully steering clear of any mention of a possible link between the government’s breach of court orders and its vote-bank interests. The News Minute has already been consistently accusing Hindus of disturbing the supposed communal harmony by refusing to look the other way when their religious beliefs and practices go for a toss.
The latest episode is merely a continuation in this direction, prioritising the consolidation of minority, particularly Muslim, vote bank above all else. However, the question is how far these political parties are prepared to go in pursuit of their demented agenda, trampling upon everything from Hindus to the judiciary. It also remains to be seen whether the courts will hold them accountable for such conduct or tolerate their free run.
Meanwhile, nothing has changed for the majority community, which continues to be forced to struggle for even its most basic religious rights, from Ayodhya to Thiruparankundram hill.

title: Muslim mob attacks Hindu Dalit youths in Gujarat’s Bhagal village where JeM terrorists were arrested: Atrocities case filed, but Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani remains silent – Exclusive Ground Report
description: Hindu Dalit youths were assaulted by a Muslim mob during Diwali celebrations in Gujarat’s Bhagal village, where three Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorists were arrested in July 2026. | OpIndia News
author: લિંકન સોખડિયા
content:
Bhagal village, located in the Palanpur taluka of Gujarat’s Banaskantha district and falling under the Vadgam Assembly constituency, has once again come into the spotlight. In July 2026, when the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) arrested eight suspected terrorists associated with the Pakistan-based terror outfit Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) from across the state, three of the eight were apprehended from this very village.
Now, another serious incident has emerged from Bhagal village, where a Muslim mob attacked young Hindu Dalits during the Hindu festival of Diwali. The OpIndia Gujarati team visited the village and spoke directly to the victims on the ground, uncovering several disturbing details about the incident.
Muslim mob abuses and assaults Dalit Hindu youths over bursting firecrackers
Speaking exclusively to OpIndia, one of the victims narrated the sequence of events and said that the incident took place at around 10 PM on the night of the 8th. Several children and young men were bursting Diwali firecrackers in an open public space at the village square.
The victim said:
“We were bursting firecrackers in a public space in the village when some members of the Muslim community sitting near a shop opposite us stopped us and said, ‘If you want to celebrate Diwali, go home and celebrate it.’ We explained to them that this was an open public space in the village and not anyone’s private property. Just as you celebrate Eid, we celebrate our Diwali. However, the Muslim men sitting there gathered in a mob and started hurling abuses and making derogatory remarks about our caste and Hindu religion.”
According to the victim, several individuals, including Faheem, Owais Patel and Anas Patel, approached them from behind and launched an assault. When the victim’s friends rushed to rescue him, they too were subjected to physical violence.
The injured youth was taken to the civil hospital for treatment. Subsequently, a police complaint was filed under various provisions, including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Acting on the complaint, the police arrested the accused.
Lights switched off and another attack planned despite police deployment
During the ground report, the victim revealed that members of the Muslim community attempted to create an atmosphere of fear in the village even on the day after the complaint was registered.
The victim said:
“The next day, police personnel were deployed in the village to ensure that people could burst firecrackers. Despite the police presence, these elements switched off the streetlights in the area and prepared to create a disturbance and launch another attack. However, since a police contingent was present at the spot, they could not carry out the assault. Even now, we are being threatened and pressured with warnings that we could be falsely implicated in criminal cases.”
Victims reveal pressure against Hindu festivals amid changing population dynamics
Speaking about the situation in the village, the victim said that this was not the first such incident in Bhagal. He revealed that since the Muslim community constitutes a larger share of the village’s population, members of the Hindu community have repeatedly faced pressure during weddings and festivals over bursting firecrackers.
“They always try to pressure us by saying that we should not speak against them and that we must not burst firecrackers,” the victim told OpIndia.
Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani, who speaks about Dalit rights, remains silent
Bhagal village falls under the Vadgam Assembly constituency, represented by Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani. The victims expressed disappointment that Mevani, who frequently raises the issue of Dalit rights and justice in his political campaigns across the country, has taken no concrete steps following the assault on Dalit youths in his own constituency.
The victim told OpIndia:
“Our area falls under the Vadgam Assembly constituency, and Jignesh Mevani is our MLA. Despite this incident being reported in newspapers and the media, he has neither visited us nor taken any concrete action so far.”
Why are Dalit community’s rights and dignity being sidelined for vote-bank politics?
The ground report from Bhagal village raises several serious questions. In a state like Gujarat, which is generally considered peaceful and has a robust law-and-order machinery, it is concerning that members of the Hindu community should have to seek someone’s permission to burst Diwali firecrackers in a public square in their own village simply because of changing population dynamics.
The incident has also brought into focus what the report describes as the double standards of politicians who raise slogans of ‘Jai Bhim-Jai Meem’. When the accused belong to a particular vote bank, even an incident involving an assault on Dalit youths and a complaint under the SC/ST Atrocities Act appears to receive little attention from Vadgam MLA Jignesh Mevani.
The swift action taken by the Gujarat Police and the deployment of security personnel reportedly prevented a major incident the following day. However, it is imperative that strict action be taken against those responsible so that a strong message is sent against such acts of intimidation and communal aggression.

title: Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam row: With its review petition, TVK government demonstrates its intent to go any extent to appease Muslims and suppress Hindu rights
description: In Tamil Nadu, the CM C Joseph Vijay-led TVK government has moved a review petition on 22nd November against the recent Supreme Court order allowing Hindus to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill on 24th November.  | OpIndia News
author: Shraddha Pandey
content:
Political secularism is so inextricably enmeshed in Muslim appeasement and Hindu neglect that governments helmed by ‘secular’ parties go to any lengths to ensure that Hindu rights are crushed. The excuse is almost always the ‘greater good’ of society, maintenance of ‘communal harmony’, ‘law and order ‘, and whatnot. In Tamil Nadu, the CM C Joseph Vijay-led TVK government has moved a review petition on 22nd November against the recent Supreme Court order allowing Hindus to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill on 24th November.
Supreme Court allows lighting of Karthigai Deepam atop the Thiruparankundram Hill in Madurai
On 20th November, the Supreme Court allowed the lighting of ‘Karthigai Deepam’ atop the Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai, during the Karthigai Deepam festival on November 24, 2026.
A Bench comprising Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi passed the order with the condition that only authorised persons from the Devasthanam (temple administration) and government officials will be able to conduct the lamp lighting ceremony.
The court granted the interim relief considering the present circumstances. It noted that if the lighting of the lamp was not allowed on the festival, no subsequent relief would be able to make up for that.
However, the court emphasised that the permission was a one-time measure for this year’s festival alone. The Bench further cautioned that the permission creates no right of custom, access or ownership regarding the hill.
“At this stage, it is neither necessary nor appropriate to express any opinion on the competing claims,” the bench said.
Muslims fume over Supreme Court allowing one-time lighting of Karthigai Deepam, TVK government rushes to file review petition
As soon as the Supreme Court granted one-time permission for lighting of Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon atop the Thiruparankundram Hill, the ruling ‘secular’ Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government raised objections.
The opposition parties, except the BJP, opposed the Supreme Court ruling.
Demonstrating their vehemence for upholding secularism at the cost of trampling over Hindu sentiments, the opposition parties, including the DMK, accused the TVK government of delay in filing a review petition.
The Congress party, which is an alliance partner in the TVK-led government, also defended the review petition, citing communal harmony.
Meanwhile, the CPI and CPI(M) welcomed the petition and called the Supreme Court ruling ‘erroneous’.
It was only the BJP and AIADMK spokespersons who condemned the TVK government’s review petition.
The TVK is reported to be holding a meeting of MLAs of its alliance parties at its official residence tonight over the Deepam issue.
Such is the state of affairs in Tamil Nadu that there is a very thin Hindu-side representation in Tamil Nadu politics, with most mainstream political parties constantly engaging in a competition of outmanoeuvring each other in being anti-Hindu.
Why TVK government filed review petition even though the Supreme Court ruling granted only one-time permission for lighting the Karthigai Deepam?
The Supreme Court ruling has granted only a one-time permission to light the Deepam, and yet the TVK government and the allied and opposed political parties alike have been charged up to prevent the Hindu ritual.
The question arises: Why? What is the real chagrin of the TVK government?
In its review petition, the HR&CE Commissioner under the TVK government has contended that granting one-time permission amounts to granting final relief at the interlocutory stage itself.
It asks whether the Supreme Court should have issued a mandatory interim direction without the petitioners establishing a strong prima facie case and demonstrating that the balance of convenience favoured them.
The petition invoked provisions of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
It highlighted that under Section 28(1), trustees are responsible for administering the affairs of religious institutions. Section 63(e) empowers the Joint Commissioner to inquire into and decide questions concerning established usage in a religious institution.
The TVK government’s review petition says that the question of where the Hindu temple’s traditional lamp should be lit must be addressed through the appropriate statutory and institutional process instead of determining it through an interim judicial direction.
It also argued that there is no established customary or legal right to light the lamp at the stone pillar atop the hill.
The review petition also claims that the Hindu petitioners have not presented documentary evidence establishing that the location was historically used for the ceremony.
The TVK government essentially expressed its apprehension that granting even one-time permission for lighting the traditional lamp, Karthigai Deepam, would set a precedent for future claims.
It says that allowing the lighting of the traditional lamp can be interpreted as the Supreme Court’s validation of the same and, by extension, the claim laid by the petitioners.
Pertinently, the review petition is worried about the Deepathoon’s proximity to a nearby Islamic shrine named Sikandar Badhusha Dargah.
The CM C Joseph Vijay-led government is concerned that lighting a traditional Hindu lamp at this spot close to a Dargah could pose a risk of disturbing communal harmony.
These, however, are technical answers. The real answer to the question about why the TVK government is against a one-time order lies in the motive that has birthed this whole pushback against the Supreme Court order.
The real chagrin of the TVK and the other ‘secular’ parties is not any legal overreach but inherent bias against Hindus and ideological-political compulsion to appease Muslims.
The Supreme Court order is narrow: one lighting, one day festival, with no ruling on title.
And yet, the government still moved to stay the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam atop the Thiruparankundram Hill, with hours to go.
This indicates that the government has an objection to the ritual itself. If the lamp is lit and the TVK government ensures unquestioned implementation of the court order, it will end up upsetting Muslims.
In fact, this whole ‘communal harmony will be disrupted’ argument put forth by Muslim-appeasing pretentious ‘secular’ parties, not only in this case, but in general, essentially means that if Hindus do not relinquish their believed religious rights even if they have a court ruling in their favour, Muslims might get upset, and possibly to the extent that they might turn violent and exercise street veto.
Remember, before and after the Supreme Court order on the Ayodhya Ram Janmabhoomi dispute case, Islamo-leftists continuously gaslighted Hindus for seeking legal remedy for reclaiming their temple.
From the Ram Janmabhoomi Movement to the struggle for Kashi Vishwanath, Krishna Janmabhoomi and many other Hindu temples encroached upon, repurposed or destroyed by Muslims, Hindus have constantly been vilified for even approaching courts to reclaim what they believe are their temples.
Arguments change: ‘instead of a temple, we should build schools, hospitals’, ‘instead of developing scientific temper, communal tensions are being stoked through manoeuvres to reclaim old temples’, and whatnot.
This is true in other contexts as well.
However, what doesn’t change is constant, direct, indirect, rhetorical or in the form of actions, reminder to the Hindu community that it is solely their responsibility to adjust their religious beliefs, festivals, traditions and suppress their religiosity to preserve ‘communal harmony’, ‘secularism’, and ‘peace ‘, while the Muslims are not required to shoulder this burden.
Just weeks back, the Islamo-leftist coterie was working overtime to advocate allowing Muslim men in Garba events during Navratri because they believe that the festival represents ‘inclusivity’, which, somehow for them, is incomplete without Muslim representation.
If a movie like Chhaava shows the atrocities committed by the Mughal tyrant Aurangzeb against Chhatrapati Sambhaji Maharaj and Muslims somehow get offended and run riots against Hindus in Maharashtra, Islamo-leftists blame the movie, the producer, and the actors but not Muslim intolerance.
Congress opposed Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon during the DMK era, and it continues to do so when in alliance with TVK
The Congress party, though only a small alliance partner with 5 seats, has publicly opposed the lighting of Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon. Its spokesperson, Manickam Tagore, is reported to have said that the RSS, Hindu Munnani, the BJP and “the BJP’s B-team like Annamalai” want to create ‘communal tension’.
“The intention of the govt is very clear: we don’t want to disturb the communal harmony and goodwill in Tamil Nadu, while the RSS, Hindu Munnani, the BJP, and the BJP’s B-team like Annamalai all want to create communal tension in Tamil Nadu. We are all standing here in Thiruparankundram,” Tagore said.
Congress had taken a similar position when it was a partner in the previous DMK government.
The Congress party and its leaders, particularly Rahul Gandhi, have in recent years been trying desperately to portray themselves as greater and truer Hindus than the ‘political Hindus’ of the BJP.
From the controversial invocation of Lord Shiva, his Abhay Mudra in the Lok Sabha, to using sculptures depicting Shiva-Shakti as Ardhnarishwar to defend his recent man-child talk, ‘Mumma sitting in Papa’s lap’, Rahul Gandhi has been trying to show that he truly understands and stands for Hinduism.
However, his party’s vilification of Hindu Munnani and the extended Hindu community for seeking legal remedy for lighting the traditional lamp at Deepathoon shows that the Congress’s stance and rhetoric on issues concerning Hindus change in states as per political convenience.
Decades back, cutting poonool or Janeu, smashing idols of Hindu deities by Periyarists was glorified as a fight for equality, social justice and freedom from superstition. Now opposing Karthigai Deepam at Deepathoon is being portrayed as not an anti-Hindu act but an act of preserving ‘communal harmony’.
This is how conveniently opposing Hindu causes and interests is packaged and presented as a struggle to protect secularism, tolerance, communal harmony, the idea of India, and whatnot.
After Hindus successfully reclaimed the Ayodhya Ram Mandir, the Islamo-leftist coterie lives in constant fear that another religious or civilisational victory, big or small, would only bolster the motivations of the Hindu community to reverse more and more historical wrongs.
Thus, even a strictly one-time court order, a petition demanding an ASI survey of a historical site and even rhetorical expression of the Hindu intent not to forfeit their believed rights anymore, is unsettling and unacceptable for the anti-Hindu and Muslim-appeasing political-ideological cabal.
The Karthigai Deepam dispute
The litigation stems from a dispute concerning the Thirupparankundram hill in Madurai, Tamil Nadu. The hill accommodates three religious sites relating to Hindus, Jains and Muslims.
At its foothills is the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple, one of the six sacred abodes of Lord Murugan.
The hilltop is home to the Sikandar Badusha Avuliya Dargah, a shrine associated with the Sufi saint Sikandar Badusha. In addition to these, the hill also contains ancient Jain caves, inscriptions and rock beds.
The hill has long been associated with Hindu traditions. The fresh dispute arose last year after Hindu devotees, who wanted to light the Hindu ceremonial lamp (Karthigai Deepam) atop the hill, faced opposition from people from the Muslim community and the Tamil Nadu government.
The Muslims and the government opposed the lamp lighting on the stone pillar located atop the hill, citing the stone pillar’s proximity to the Sikandar Badusha Dargah.
In December 2025, a single-judge Bench of Justice G R Swaminathan allowed the Hindu devotees’ plea and directed the Arulmigu Subramania Swamy Temple administration to light the lamp at the stone pillar called Deepathoon.
Thereafter, the matter reached the Madras High Court last year. A single-judge bench of Justice G R Swaminathan allowed the Hindu devotees’ plea and directed the Arulmigu Subramania Swamy Temple administration to light the lamp at the stone pillar in December.
Subsequently, a Division Bench of the High Court upheld the Single Bench’s decision in January 2026. The present order comes in the appeals filed by the Tamil Nadu government against the decision of the Division Bench of the High Court.
TVK’s Muslim and Christian appeasement policies
The TVK government in Tamil Nadu has been accused of squandering state funds on freebies and Muslim appeasement-driven schemes even as the state’s financial health is deteriorating.
Recently, the TVK government announced that the state government will cover the full undergraduate tuition fees for Muslim female students admitted under the government quota in government, government-aided, and self-financing colleges. For this, the government allocated ₹20 crore.
Minister A M Shahjahan also announced the expansion of the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board scholarship for Muslim girls, from Classes 1-8 to Classes 9-10 at ₹2,000 per year. The scheme is expected to benefit 41,384 Muslim schoolgirls for Rs 8.28 crore.
An announcement was also made about a ‘minorities’ women’s college in Chennai through the Waqf Board, with an initial grant of ₹2.45 crore.
Moreover, the Vijay government has also announced a ₹100 crore interest-free revolving fund for loans to develop income-generating assets like marriage halls, commercial complexes, etc. on Muslim and Christian properties.
The state government will also construct a new headquarters for the Tamil Nadu Waqf Board at an estimated cost of ₹40 crore. The administrative grant for the state Waqf Board will also be raised to ₹5 crore.

title: How To Think About Punjab Politics
description: There is a territory in which the powerful landed class dominates its politics through leaders and resources to dominate communities organised around
author: Abhishek Kumar
content:
Punjab
Abhishek Kumar
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 12:58 PM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
There is a territory in which the powerful landed class dominates its politics through leaders and resources to dominate communities organised around different demographies.
In this area, religious clerics have power over elected representatives. For reasons other than loss of legitimacy, governments regularly use subsidies and cash transfers to keep their constituencies satisfied. Even parties that promise to dismantle the old arrangement eventually find themselves governing through it.
It is a system in which changing the party in power rarely means changing the people or institutions that exercise power. This is the version of politics that is similar to the Pakistani political order of the last few decades.
However, one can argue that the description above closely matches the reality of India's Punjab as well. Across the international border, the two Punjabs and by extension Pakistan share a political inheritance in which land, religious authority and patronage have shaped the relationship between voters and political parties.
Their institutions are different on paper, but pressures on elected governments from unelected centres of powers are remarkably similar.
On 15 June 2026, the Akal Takht declared Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann 'Guru Dokhi' and 'Khalsa Panth virodhi', accusing him of misleading the Sikh religious institution over a purportedly objectionable video. Mann disputed the Takht's findings about the video and alleged that a Canada-based associate of Sukhbir Singh Badal had arranged to impersonate him.
The rebuke came just two months after the Punjab Assembly had unanimously passed a law prescribing imprisonment of up to life and fines of up to Rs 25 lakh for sacrilege against the Guru Granth Sahib.
But the legislation itself brought AAP into conflict with the Akal Takht, which objected that the government had legislated on Sikh religious affairs without consulting the Panth or its institutions. It summoned Sikh legislators across party lines to explain their support for the law.
Apparently, the party which promised to end Punjab's old politics was now being judged by some of the oldest rules of that politics.
In Punjab, governments have changed, but the larger socio-political order within which they operate has proved considerably more durable.
The AAP broke the Congress and Shiromani Akali Dal's alternating hold on government in 2022, but failed to displace the interests that had shaped their governments.
With the exceptions of Giani Zail Singh, a Ramgarhia Sikh, Charanjit Singh Channi, a Ramdasia Sikh, and last-minute arrangements from the Indian National Congress (INC), Punjab's chief ministers have overwhelmingly come from the Jat Sikh community.
Punjab politics’ oldest rule is that a government governs with the consent of a Jat Sikh landed order. Every government in Chandigarh, regardless of party, has had to accommodate its interests through land policy, subsidised farm power and deference to the religious institutions that police its boundaries.
AAP came to power in 2022 as new, third force in what was a bipolar field. It has since retained farm-power subsidies, extended cash transfers to women and seen its own legislators summoned before the Akal Takht's Jathedar.
Varying estimates suggest that Jat Sikhs account for an estimated one-fifth of Punjab's population, making them the largest unitary community in the state. Scheduled Castes, regularly referred to as Dalits comprise above 31.94 per cent of state population, highest among any state in India.
Despite that Dalits wield very little influence over the state, its policy and decision making, as compared to Jats. One reason is that the Dalit is an umbrella category and contain a lot of internal differences while Jat Sikhs are one community.
They dominate agricultural landholding and have historically supplied much of the state's political leadership.
Comparatively, sitting at nearly 31.94 per cent of the population, Dalits own only 3.5 per cent of private agricultural land.
This has a limiting effect on multiple reform agendas of various governments.
For instance, the state's biggest urbanisation plan in a decade failed when the government set the terms, and came back only when it let landowners choose. In June 2025, the AAP government notified a scheme to pool 65,533 acres from about 164 villages around 21 cities for housing and industry.
Farm unions, opposition parties and village panchayats opposed it. Village after village passed resolutions against the scheme and barred AAP leaders from entering. The government withdrew it on 11 August.
In November 2025, the government brought the scheme back as an optional one. Farmers could choose between developed plots and compensation under the 2013 land acquisition law.
Before this supposedly economic challenge to the dominance of large land-owners, INC tried to challenge it on symbolism on the eve of 2022 election by appointing Charanjit Singh Channi, a Dalit, as chief minister. Despite that, data from Lokniti-CSDS post-poll survey suggest that only 27 per cent of Dalit Sikhs voted for the INC, against 46 per cent for AAP. INC fell from 21 Scheduled Caste-reserved seats in 2017 to five in 2022, while Channi lost both constituencies he contested.
AAP subsequently appointed another Jat Sikh, Bhagwant Mann, as chief minister, even though it got support from all communities.
Before AAP, the Shiromani Akali Dal(SAD) represented the state's Sikh political constituency, particularly its rural and dominant Jat Sikh base, while the BJP drew much of its support from Hindus. Their alliance allowed the two parties to combine their constituencies without competing directly for the same political space.
The SAD-BJP alliance won the Punjab Assembly elections in 1997, 2007 and 2012. In 2012, the SAD secured 56 seats and the BJP 12, returning the incumbent government to power for the first time in Punjab's post-reorganisation history.
The alliance's electoral success couldn’t conceal growing discontent with the Badal government's handling of Sikh religious affairs. In 2015, for instance, Punjab erupted in protests over the Bargari Sacrilege case.
The government's mishandling of the incidents provoked widespread anger among Sikhs. The controversy was compounded by the September 2015 pardon granted by the Akal Takht to Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim, which was subsequently withdrawn.
Sukhbir Singh Badal, then deputy chief minister and home minister, was seen to prioritise politics over Sikh religious sentiments. The incidents damaged the Badals' credibility among the very Panthic voters who had traditionally supported the party. In 2017, SAD's tally fell from 56 to 15 seats and its vote share dropped to 25.2 per cent.
After the setback, several senior leaders like Ranjit Singh Brahmpura, Sukhdev Singh Dhindsa, Rattan Singh Ajnala and Sewa Singh Sekhwan, blamed the Badal family for centralising control of the party and its failure to address the sacrilege controversy.
The party's difficulties deepened in 2020 when the Badal-led SAD broke its alliance with the BJP over the farm laws.
In June 2024, following another poor performance in the Lok Sabha election, a group of senior leaders led by Bibi Jagir Kaur, Prem Singh Chandumajra and Parminder Singh Dhindsa revolted against Sukhbir Badal and demanded his resignation.
The internal rebellion eventually produced another split in August 2025, when former Akal Takht jathedar Giani Harpreet Singh became president of the Shiromani Akali Dal (Punar Surjit), a breakaway group claiming to represent the original Akali Dal.
The fragmentation has left the Badal-led SAD competing with several rival organisations for the Panthic vote, most famous of whom is Amritpal Singh's Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De). In August 2024, the Akal Takht declared Sukhbir Badal 'tankhaiya', or guilty of religious misconduct, over decisions taken during his tenure between 2007 and 2017.
However, the 2025 Tarn Taran Assembly bypoll showed that the Badal-led SAD could still command the Panthic votes despite the emergence of rival Panthic organisations in this constituency. Tarn Taran falls within the Khadoor Sahib parliamentary constituency, where Amritpal Singh had won the 2024 Lok Sabha election by nearly two lakh votes.
Contrarily, SAD's alliance partner BJP, despite its reputation as a saffron party and remaining a predominantly Hindu partner, has not been able to replace INC as a dominant force among Punjabi Hindus, which constitute approximately 38.5 per cent of Punjab's electorate.
Lokniti-CSDS surveys show that the INC consistently secured more than 45 per cent of non-Dalit Hindu votes in Assembly elections between 2002 and 2017. The division of Sikh and Hindu support between the SAD and INC, with the BJP as the Akalis' junior alliance partner had sustained Punjab's bipolar political arrangement for a long period.
The Hindu vote was often decisive in swinging elections between the INC and the SAD-BJP alliance.
The 2022 elections proved to be a crucial turning point when AAP ended Punjab's two-party alternation, winning 92 of 117 seats with 42.01 per cent of the vote.
AAP had mobilised voters around corruption, unemployment and poor public services, while promising financial assistance to women and continued subsidies for households and farmers.
It gave the BJP room to reconsider its position regarding dependency on SAD in Punjab. AAP's success showed that voters were willing to move beyond the established political alignments.
In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, contesting alone except for smaller allies, the BJP secured 18.56 per cent of the vote, its highest share in Punjab, led in 23 Assembly segments and finished ahead of the SAD in 45.
Meanwhile, AAP saw its vote share fall to 26.02 per cent and won three Lok Sabha seats. However, its performance in Assembly by-elections was considerably stronger. It won six of the seven held after taking office.
AAP subsequently won 218 of 347 zila parishad zones in December 2025 and 958 of 1,977 municipal wards in the May 2026 civic elections, seen as poor performance for the party in charge. The party's organisational position suffered another setback on 24 April 2026, when seven (six from Punjab) of its ten Rajya Sabha MPs joined the BJP.
In government, AAP has continued with a Jat Sikh chief minister, continued free electricity for farmers and 300 free units for households, and introduced cash transfers for women. It also passed a stricter sacrilege law unanimously, something which Punjab’s established political order would always be proud of.
Even so, sacrilege cases in Punjab rarely end in a conviction. Punjab Police registered 597 cases between 2015 and early 2026, and only 44 led to one. The principal 2015 cases took nearly seven years to produce a conviction: in July 2022, a Moga court sentenced three Dera Sacha Sauda followers to three years in prison and acquitted two others.
The AAP government passed its own sacrilege law at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi in April 2026. Sukhbir Badal calls the record a failure of AAP. Slow courts and political blame together make a sacrilege accusation particularly dangerous for people with little social or political influence.
In Pakistan, Human Rights Watch's June 2025 report, A Conspiracy to Grab the Land, documented how accusations of blasphemy were used against poor people and religious minorities to force them out of their homes and seize property in prominent places like Lahore, Gujranwala, Kasur, Sheikhupura and Islamabad.
In all such cases, the damage is done long before a court establishes guilt.
A harsher law makes an accusation a more powerful weapon. People, especially in a mob, look to the state's laws to justify their own actions. The more severe the punishment the law prescribes, the surer vigilantes feel in taking justice into their own hands.
The line between a breach of maryada (religious protocol) and deliberate sacrilege is blurring. There is little room left to weigh circumstances, intent and the nature of the act.
Political parties now compete for religious legitimacy at a time when their own record on drugs, links to criminal networks, drinking and public welfare is seen as out of step with Sikh values. That gap between what is expected of leaders and what they have done has made religious endorsement and censure central to political competition.
When INC leader Amarinder Singh Raja Warring touched the hair knots of two Sikh children, Sukhbir Badal accused him of beadbi. AAP leaders, including Bhagwant Mann, joined in. The INC hit back with Badal's own record: the 2015 Bargari incidents, the pardon to Gurmeet Ram Rahim and his conduct towards the Akal Takht.
The Panthic fringe has used this to build a base. Amritpal Singh won the Khadoor Sahib Lok Sabha seat in 2024. With fellow MP Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa, he launched the Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De) at the Maghi Mela on 14 January 2025. In April 2026, the party named him its chief ministerial candidate for 2027, though he remains in Dibrugarh jail under the National Security Act.
Cheap internet means these rows and gestures now reach far more people than before. Mainstream parties, already cornered on morality, cannot afford to look less committed to the cause. This anxiety probably led the Punjab Assembly to amend the 2008 law regulating the printing and distribution of the Guru Granth Sahib and add much harsher criminal penalties.
However, the Akal Takht and the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee objected because the government had not consulted them before introducing the legislation. Their objections include the terminology used in the law, the registration of every copy of the Guru Granth Sahib, the identification of its custodians and the statutory responsibilities imposed on the SGPC.
The Takht also argued that provisions governing the scripture could place ordinary Sikh households, granthis, panthis and sewadars within an unnecessary legal framework. It also wanted dera chiefs to face an FIR if their followers committed sacrilege. Several deras have sizable Dalit followings, particularly among communities that have faced discrimination within Punjab's society.
For many Dalits, these deras offer religious spaces and a sense of social belonging outside traditional Sikh institutional structures. Their followers also constitute an important electoral constituency that political parties cannot easily ignore. Holding dera chiefs legally accountable could have brought AAP into conflict with institutions that command considerable support among Dalit voters.
On 29 June, Sikh legislators from all parties appeared before the Akal Takht's Jathedar, where many of them admitted that they had not read the legislation before voting for it. The government submitted a written response in July, but the Takht rejected it and appointed a five-member committee to negotiate amendments.
The politics of sacrilege supplies the emotional force that holds this order together, but the politics of the treasury sustains it. Rising debt, entrenched subsidies, free electricity and cash transfers keep the existing landed power structure financially and politically intact.
Free electricity for farmers was introduced in January 1997 by INC chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, initially for farmers owning up to seven acres. When Parkash Singh Badal took office the following month, he extended the benefit to all farmers. Amarinder Singh withdrew the subsidy in 2002, citing the state's financial condition, but restored it in September 2005.
Every major party has since defended the policy, making free agricultural electricity one of Punjab's most enduring political commitments.
AAP extended the subsidy system with its promise of 300 free units of electricity every month to domestic consumers.
The 2026-27 budget allocates Rs 7,715 crore for agricultural electricity subsidies and another Rs 5,771 crore for domestic consumers.
The same budget introduced a new cash transfer for women. The Mukh Mantri Mawan Dhian Satikar Yojana provides Rs 1,000 a month to women above 18 and Rs 1,500 to Scheduled Caste women.
Free farm electricity mainly benefits landowners who run tubewells. The domestic power subsidy reaches electricity consumers across the state, and the new scheme pays women directly. None of this changes who owns land, which remains a major source of inequality in rural Punjab. The subsidies and cash transfers are a stopgap: they compensate groups without land but leave their position in the rural economy unchanged.
The law does give Dalits a claim to some land. The Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, reserves one-third of cultivable panchayat land for Scheduled Castes, leased through annual auctions. For decades, upper-caste farmers took much of it through proxy Dalit bidders. Since 2014, the Zameen Prapti Sangharsh Committee has organised village-level resistance to this. It has won some ground, mainly in southern Punjab, but its reach is small against the scale of landholding inequality.
These commitments are also straining Punjab's finances. The 2026-27 budget puts committed expenditure at Rs 90,335 crore, or 72 per cent of revenue receipts. Capital outlay is Rs 18,381 crore. The fiscal deficit is projected at 4.1 per cent of GSDP, above the 3 per cent limit set by the Sixteenth Finance Commission.
The Union finance ministry placed Punjab's debt-to-GSDP ratio at 46.6 per cent in March 2025, the second highest among states after Arunachal Pradesh. In its 2026-27 budget documents, the Punjab government put the ratio at 44.77 per cent, Finance Minister Harpal Singh Cheema has argued that 85 per cent of government borrowing has gone towards servicing debt inherited from previous administrations.
The government points to improvements in its revenue position by citing its own tax revenue increase from Rs 37,327 crore in 2021-22 to Rs 57,919 crore in 2024-25. However, the CAG has warned that economic growth alone may not be sufficient to meet the state's financial obligations.
Way Forward
The 2027 Assembly election will test the political arrangements that have shaped Punjab for decades.
The BJP and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) are back in an alliance.
In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, BJP and SAD together polled 31.98 per cent, against 26.30 per cent for the INC and 26.02 per cent for AAP. The return of the Akali Dal to the NDA restores the Sikh-Hindu coalition that governed Punjab for two decades.
Waris Punjab De and the Akali factions will compete for the Panthic vote, while the INC will seek to recover its Hindu and Dalit support. AAP will rely on its welfare programmes and its record in local elections.
AAP's victory in 2022 changed who governs Punjab. The party that replaces it in 2027, if at all, will inherit the same landed order, the same politics around sacrilege and a budget already committed to substantial recurring expenditure.
The question facing Punjab's parties is whether any of them is prepared to confront even one of these arrangements. So far, no major party has made confronting any of them central to its politics.
Abhishek is Staff Writer at Swarajya.

title: Indian Army's Team Mountain Eagles Marks Aviation Milestone With Successful Landing And Refuelling On NH-754K In Gujarat
description: The Indian Army's Team Mountain Eagles achieved a historic milestone yesterday when four aircraft successfully landed and refuelled on NH-754K near Pa
author: Swarajya Staff
content:
Defence
Swarajya Staff
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 08:56 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
The Indian Army's Team Mountain Eagles achieved a historic milestone yesterday when four aircraft successfully landed and refuelled on NH-754K near Patan district in Gujarat.
The formation, comprising two microlight aircraft and two powered hang gliders, demonstrated the first-ever landing of such a formation on a national highway or expressway in India.
The expedition team from the Army Adventure Nodal Centre at the Military College of Telecommunication Engineering in Mhow, Madhya Pradesh, took off from Kandla Airport and landed on the Amritsar-Jamnagar Expressway near Bakutra Toll Plaza in Santalpur Tehsil.
Part of the ongoing "Wings of Valour and Unity" Expedition, the operation showcased the capability of national highways to serve as alternative emergency landing grounds for small aircraft.
The demonstration highlighted the strong civil-military cooperation, with the National Highways Authority of India and local civil administration coordinating all arrangements.
Officials from NHAI, including a director, along with the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tehsildar and local police authorities personally supervised the operation. The event marks a significant achievement for Team Mountain Eagles in demonstrating precision flying skills.
NH-754K forms part of the strategic Amritsar-Jamnagar Economic Corridor, a vital infrastructure project enhancing regional connectivity in the Kutch region.
The successful landing and refuelling operation underscores the dual-use potential of India's expanding highway network, supporting both civilian connectivity and national defence preparedness during emergencies or strategic requirements.

title: Thiruparankundram: How TVK Government Made A Mockery Of Supreme Court's Order
description: On the sacred evening of Karthigai Deepam, the lamp burned at the customary Uchi Pillaiyar Mandapam, while the ancient stone Deepathoon atop Thirupara
author: K Balakumar
content:
Tamil Nadu
K Balakumar
Nov 25, 2026 | Updated 05:44 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
On the sacred evening of Karthigai Deepam, the lamp burned at the customary Uchi Pillaiyar Mandapam, while the ancient stone Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill remained plunged in darkness.
That darkness is not merely the absence of a flame. It is a monument to administrative bad faith and open judicial defiance by Tamil Nadu's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government.
Four days ago, on 20 November, a Supreme Court bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi passed a crystal-clear, tightly calibrated interim order permitting a restricted team authorised by the temple administration to light the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon on 24 November as a one-time measure.
The apex court left zero room for ambiguity: no public processions, no slogans, full protection by the Archaeological Survey of India, undisturbed worship at the dargah, and even the explicit option to deploy central forces if the state required assistance.
Yet instead of honouring the highest court in the land, the TVK administration unleashed a textbook display of State-sponsored obstruction. First, the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) Commissioner rushed to file a last-minute review petition to stall the order.
Simultaneously, district authorities clamped down with sweeping prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), sealing off access, detaining devotees, and turning a sacred festival into a police state.
When urgent petitions challenging this heavy-handed blockade reached the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Monday, Justices G R Swaminathan and M D Sumathi tore into the State's disingenuous posture.
Summoning the Madurai District Collector and police brass in person, the Bench reminded the administration of the basic constitutional truth under Article 144: the mere pendency of a review petition does not suspend a binding Supreme Court order, and all authorities are constitutionally mandated to act in aid of the apex court.
Cornered by the judges' sharp questioning, senior counsel for the Collector assured the High Court in open session that authorities were taking steps to comply and would not use the review petition as an excuse for non-compliance.
Hours later, when the decisive moment arrived at dusk, that courtroom assurance proved to be worth less than the paper it was written on. The Deepathoon was never lit.
The TVK government did not merely fail to implement the Supreme Court's directive; it brazenly misled the Madras High Court while running down the clock until the auspicious window passed.
Settled History, Deliberately Distorted
To justify this institutional sabotage, the State machinery and its ideological echo chamber will talk about how temple authorities did not give the names of the representatives to accompany the lamp-lighting at the Deepathoon.
They will also peddle the fiction that lighting a lamp at the Deepathoon is a newly invented provocation that threatens communal harmony. Both history and over a century of judicial precedent, however, expose this narrative as a fabrication.
Thiruparankundram is the foremost of Lord Murugan's Arupadai Veedu (six sacred abodes). The hill bears the layered imprint of Tamil Nadu's spiritual past, housing the ancient Subramania Swamy Temple, eighth-century Jain rock-cut caves and the Sikandar Badusha Dargah near the summit. Yet the legal title to the hill has been settled for nearly a hundred years.
In a landmark 1920 civil suit decided in 1923, and decisively affirmed by the Privy Council in 1931, courts conclusively established that the unoccupied portions of Thiruparankundram Hill and the pilgrim pathways belong to the Subramania Swamy Temple Devasthanam, while carving out and protecting specific pockets around the mosque and its access steps for Muslim worship.
The Deepathoon, located on the lower peak roughly 50 metres away from the dargah, sits squarely within temple territory.
When the State counsel attempted to muddy the waters by insinuating that the carved stone pillar was merely a British-era survey marker or a relic of obscure provenance rather than a sacred lamp post, the Madras High Court examined the physical evidence directly last year.
The Division Bench documented the carved cavity at the crown of the pillar explicitly designed to hold oil and a wick, affirmed its identity as the Deepathoon, and ruled unequivocally that the Deepathoon area belongs to the temple and that lighting the Karthigai Deepam there is a protected religious practice.
The dispute was never about encroaching on the dargah. It was about whether Hindus could light a ceremonial lamp on land indisputably belonging to their own temple.
Mainstreaming Contempt: A Threat To Constitutional Order
Even more alarming than bureaucratic foot-dragging is the toxic political climate surrounding this episode. In the run-up to Karthigai Deepam, large segments of Tamil Nadu's political class and fringe outfits openly issued public calls to defy the Supreme Court's order.
The breakdown of civic restraint was so severe that the Madras High Court had to pass an extraordinary John Doe injunction restraining members of the public from inciting disobedience against the apex court.
When politicians, activists and officeholders normalise the idea that Supreme Court verdicts can be vetoed on the streets through threats of law and order disruption, they strike at the very foundation of constitutional democracy.
The rule of law cannot survive in a State where executive compliance is selective: enforced ruthlessly against peaceful devotees seeking darshan, yet paralysed the moment ideological allies or vocal pressure groups threaten unrest.
If a State government can nullify a Supreme Court order simply by refusing central security forces, imposing Section 163 bans and pleading helplessness, then constitutional guarantees under Articles 25 and 26 cease to be rights and become revocable state favours.
New Regime, Same Anti-Hindu Reflex
The bitterest irony of tonight's betrayal lies in the political mandate that brought the TVK to power.
During the 2025 Thiruparankundram standoff, the previous DMK regime deployed the exact same playbook of Section 163 bans and administrative stonewalling, prompting Justice Swaminathan to warn that permitting officers to defy court orders would invite anarchy. Widespread Hindu anger over asymmetrical secularism and State control of temples played a role in the DMK's 2026 electoral rout.
Voters who backed Chief Minister Vijay and the TVK in search of a clean break from Dravidian-era hostility toward Hindu institutions have been handed a rude awakening.
Far from dismantling the adversarial machinery, the TVK government has adopted it wholesale and, if anything, gone one step further by flouting not just a High Court bench, but an explicit order of the Supreme Court of India and its own pledge to the judiciary.
Accountability cannot stop at the Madurai Collectorate or the HR&CE Commissioner's office. District officials do not orchestrate multi-agency blockades, refuse central forces and renege on High Court undertakings without political sanction from the very top.
By leaving the Deepathoon unlit on Monday night, the TVK government has illuminated something far more revealing: its deep-seated contempt for the judiciary, for settled historical title and for the fundamental rights of Tamil Nadu's Hindus.
If the Supreme Court's writ does not run atop Thiruparankundram Hill, it means the constitutional health of Tamil Nadu is in deep pits.
